articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Four Seasons Arts Four Seasons Arts, a classical music recital and chamber series in Berkeley, needs volunteer drivers to provide door-to-door transportation for subscribers in Alameda and Contra Costa counties. Concerts are held on Saturday afternoons at 3 p.m., and subscribers who use the transportation service attend 5 concerts per season. Volunteer drivers are given a pair of complimentary concert tickets and complete directions to one or two convenient stops. Volunteers can drive once or to several concerts, depending on their availability. Drivers must use a reliable, safe, and insured vehicle, have a good DMV driving record and pass a basic background check. For more information, contact Mary Jo Hudgel by phone at 845-4444 or by email at mjhudgel@fsarts.org. Oakland Museum Volunteering at the Oakland Museum of California gives adults and teens the chance to get more involved with a local museum, and an opportunity to learn more about the state’s rich history. The museum is always recruiting volunteers to assist with school groups, events, office work, and more. Informational sessions are offered several times a year, where museum staff discuss the various types of opportunities available. Learn more about orientation dates and apply to volunteer by visiting shiftboard.com/museumca. Prisoners Literature Project The Berkeley-based Prisoners Literature Project is an all-volunteer grassroots nonprofit that has provided free books to prisoners for over 30 years. The organization is always looking for volunteers to answer letters, send out books, learn more about the prison system, and assist with fundraising or publicity efforts. Adult volunteers are encouraged to help, and youth volunteers aged 10 through 15 are welcome with a parent or guardian overseeing their work. Visit prisonlit.org/volunteer for more information. HandsOn Bay Area HandsOn connects community members with high-quality volunteer projects through an extensive network of local nonprofits and schools in need. There are always opportunities for kids and adults to volunteer with HandsOn across a variety of industries and skill sets, with venues including food banks, community gardens, libraries, and clothing distribution centers. articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has announced the September schedule of its “Cop on the Block” program, a yearlong series of community outreach events which launched in June. It is the first scheduled walking patrol. The following patrols are scheduled through September: Monday, September 4, 8 pm Jerome Avenue between Magnolia and Keefer Court Tuesday, September 12, 1 pm Sea View Avenue between Lincoln and Hampton Sunday, September 17, 7 pm Monticello Avenue between Park and Moraga Thursday, September 28, 6:30 pm Cavenagh Court & Trestle Glen Described by the department as a program designed to bring officers out of cars and into neighborhoods, neighbors are invited to bring their questions, comments and concerns to officers as they patrol the city’s blocks on foot at selected locations and times, announced by PPD monthly. Police Captain Chris Monahan, who oversees the program, said, “We rolled out Cop on the Block as a way to encourage more non-enforcement contact with the community. It’s very casual. We plan that each week with a member of the department walking up and down the block for a minimum of half an hour and for as long as people want to chat. “We plan to keep going with the program until we cover the whole city,” he added. “Piedmont has about 145 streets and once we cover them all, a block at time, we’ll start over again. We currently plan to keep it at one officer a week. So far, the program has been very well-received; I’ve even had people call me and ask to schedule a time and date for us to visit their block.” Monahan encourages those interested in bringing Cop on the Block to their street (block patrols are scheduled 90 days in advance), or who have questions about the program, to contact him by phone at 520-3012 or by email at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov. More information on Cop on the Block events, including an interactive map of the blocks where PPD police officers will go and where they’ve been, can be found through the Piedmont Police Department’s website at bit.ly/42yYRTu. pages.text: 4 Wednesday, August 23, 2023 Local Items Cop on the Block: September schedule By Selen Ozturk The Piedmont Police Department (PPD) has announced the September schedule of its “Cop on the Block” program, a yearlong series of community outreach events which launched in June. It is the first scheduled walking patrol. The following patrols are scheduled through September: Monday, September 4, 8 pm Jerome Avenue between Magnolia and Keefer Court Tuesday, September 12, 1 pm Sea View Avenue between Lincoln and Hampton Sunday, September 17, 7 pm Monticello Avenue between Park and Moraga Thursday, September 28, 6:30 pm Cavenagh Court & Trestle Glen Described by the department as a program designed to bring officers out of cars and into neighborhoods, neighbors are invited to bring their questions, comments and concerns to officers as they patrol the city’s blocks on foot at selected locations and times, announced by PPD monthly. Police Captain Chris Monahan, who oversees the program, said, “We rolled out Cop on the Block as a way to encourage more non-enforcement contact with the community. It’s very casual. We plan that each week with a member of the department walking up and down the block for a minimum of half an hour and for as long as people want to chat. “We plan to keep going with the program until we cover the whole city,” he added. “Piedmont has about 145 streets and once we cover them all, a block at time, we’ll start over again. We currently plan to keep it at one officer a week. So far, the program has been very well-received; I’ve even had people call me and ask to schedule a time and date for us to visit their block.” Monahan encourages those interested in bringing Cop on the Block to their street (block patrols are scheduled 90 days in advance), or who have questions about the program, to contact him by phone at 520-3012 or by email at cmonahan@piedmont.ca.gov. More information on Cop on the Block events, including an interactive map of the blocks where PPD police officers will go and where they’ve been, can be found through the Piedmont Police Department’s website at bit.ly/42yYRTu. articles.text: Piedmont School District’s Wellness Center’s first Week of Wellness will run from September 20 to 27. During the week supporters who purchase an event ticket or sponsorship have access to events ranging from fitness classes at local studios to walks and outdoor activities led by Piedmont parents. The Week of Wellness is the center’s largest annual fundraiser and helps ensure that Piedmont students continue to receive the mental health support they need. The Wellness Center is a vital resource for Piedmont high school and middle school students. Counselors at the center help them manage common emotional and social challenges, including stress, depression, grief, conflicts, and substance use concerns. Approximately one-third of high school and one-quarter of middle school students receive counseling at the Wellness Center each year. Last year the Center provided over 2,000 therapy sessions to Piedmont students. To raise funds needed, the parent-run Wellness Center Support Committee is partnering with local fitness facilities and parents to create a special week of healthy activities, with events ranging from fitness classes like yoga, spin, and Zumba, to outdoor activities led by Piedmont parents. articles.text: The Beach Dads Club will host its largest annual event on Sunday, September 10, the 18th Annual Beach Dads Pancake Breakfast at Beach Elementary School, 100 Lake Avenue. The club’s new president Michael Gross helped kick off the school year with a welcome event on Thursday evening, August 17, held in Eric Pinsky’s backyard. The get together, which included beer on tap, lumpia, chicken wings and homemade cookies, brought together 50 dads to catch up after the summer and plan for the year. “A lot of these people are new to Piedmont; some just moved in last week,” said Gross. “Especially for the TK parents, we’re all going to be together for the next 14 years, so it was a good way to get to know people.” In addition to the Pancake Breakfast, the Dads Club also hosts an end-of-year BBQ and coordinates volunteering for the school. Gross was a bacon griller last year at the Pancake Breakfast, and this year he takes over as the “Padre Grande.” “Last year I looked over and saw Beach dad James Syhabout flipping pancakes and grilling bacon. He’s the owner of the restaurant Commis, and a Michelin star chef,” said Gross. Hundreds of pancakes from six grills will be flipped at the event which requires more than 40 volunteer dads, along with the help of Scout Troop 4 and music by the Carmel Quartet jazz band consisting of Beach school alums. The pancake party runs in conjunction with the Chalk Art Festival, also on the Beach Blacktop. The Beach Dads Club hosted a Welcome event on August 17. Letters to home by kids at Camp Augusta Throughout the summer the Post prints a sampling of photos of kids’ activities at Camp Augusta, Piedmont’s residential camp at Lake Vera outside Nevada City in the Sierra foothills. Founded in 1931, the camp remains a vital part of the life of hundreds of children each summer. As summer comes to a close at Camp Augusta, the staff members were ready to give it their all one last time. The evening programs were doubled, mega play stations scheduled, and during cabin acts we had the first ever oatmeal versus slime fight. With over 60 first-year campers, we were able to wow all of them with the wish, wonder, and surprise Augusta has to offer. We are trying to do as much as we can in as little time as possible. Mega playstation was brought back this year, with everything bigger, better and having never run before. We are sad that these campers have only been here a short time and have to leave, but we are glad that we made their camp time as fun as possible. Campers solved a series of puzzles, ran from rogue pirates and played games of Liar’s Dice to complete the game of Arrrrrcapelago. Campers fill up water balloons with paint to throw at each other on the wheel of doom. For cabin act, this cabin decided to destroy their counselor’s shoes by running a gauntlet on the lake field and ending with the rope swing into the lake. A pine cabin wanted to throw flaming pine cones into buckets filled with smoke bombs. As a special birthday celebration, Manzi 1 made cupcakes for their cabin members. A good cabin bonding time on the first day of the session, low ropes allows campers to have fun while also working on their team-building skills. Evening programs bring campers together, especially when completing stations as a cabin group.

articles.text: Piedmont High graduate Alexandra Clayton (2005) co-directed her first feature length film, Unpacking, in Bali in 2019. The film is showing in Mountain View on August 25 and 30 part of the Cinequest Film & Creativity Festival. Clayton also wrote, produced and acted in the indie film, with the help of PHS alums Chelsea Bangert as Graphic Designer, and Mitchell Manburg as Music Composer. Synopsis: “Six women, sold on the promise of radical transformation, travel to Bali into the hands of an influencer guru and get slapped with reality: change is messy AF. It’s awkward and earnest. It’s humor where people are taking themselves so seriously, that it’s comical – almost a cringe comedy,” said Clayton. To make this film, co-directors Michal Sinnott and Clayton asked 40 friends in the acting world if they would take two weeks to fly to Bali for filming. A dozen accepted the offer and the movie was shot in 13 days. “It’s been such a journey. I thought it was going to be something small with our friends for no money but it has been a big undertaking,” she said. After graduating from Piedmont High, Clayton went to community college and then finished her undergraduate degree at Columbia. In New York she realized that film was her passion. The Cinequest Film & Creativity Festival runs until the end of the month. pages.text: Wednesday, August 23, 2023 9 Unpacking is first feature film for PHS grad Alexandra Clayton By Jay Russell Piedmont High graduate Alexandra Clayton (2005) co-directed her first feature length film, Unpacking, in Bali in 2019. The film is showing in Mountain View on August 25 and 30 part of the Cinequest Film & Creativity Festival. Clayton also wrote, produced and acted in the indie film, with the help of PHS alums Chelsea Bangert as Graphic Designer, and Mitchell Manburg as Music Composer. Synopsis: “Six women, sold on the promise of radical transformation, travel to Bali into the hands of an influencer guru and get slapped with reality: change is messy AF. It’s awkward and earnest. It’s humor where people are taking themselves so seriously, that it’s comical – almost a cringe comedy,” said Clayton. To make this film, co-directors Michal Sinnott and Clayton asked 40 friends in the acting world if they would take two weeks to fly to Bali for filming. A dozen accepted the offer and the movie was shot in 13 days. “It’s been such a journey. I thought it was going to be something small with our friends for no money but it has been a big undertaking,” she said. After graduating from Piedmont High, Clayton went to community college and then finished her undergraduate degree at Columbia. In New York she realized that film was her passion. The Cinequest Film & Creativity Festival runs until the end of the month. articles.text: On July 27 Piedmont Council Scouts Jack Langowski, Simon March-Cunningham, and Naomi Treichler packed their Scouting gear into duffle bags and backpacks to join other U.S. Scouts at the 25th World Scout Jamboree in South Korea from August 1 to 12. The World Jamboree is held every four years. This year South Korea hosted over 40,000 Scouts representing more than 153 countries at Saemangeum in the North Jeolla province. During the first few days Piedmont Scouts spent time making friends with Scouts from all over the world through activities and meals. “We helped a Kenyan unit set up their camp next to us, had dinner with Scouts from Taiwan, the UK, and Sweden, and I had lunch with a group of Irish Scouts,” said March-Cunningham. “In fact, I just spent time this weekend talking online with a Scout from Ukraine who I met at the Jamboree.” Langowski spent time meeting Scouts and trading U.S. neckerchiefs (neckers) from other countries – a tradition at all Scout Jamborees. He used the trading as an opportunity to meet Scouts from all over the world including Peru, Namibia, Kenya, Israel, Hong Kong, the United Kingdom and Latvia, where his grandmother grew up. He also collected a necker and belt from Poland, his grandfather’s native country. Each item he brought home had its own story and special memory. Treichler’s favorite necker trade was with a Korean Scout when she went in the Korean unit camps looking for someone to trade with. “One of the Scouts seemed almost as excited as I was to trade, and the smile on his face when I gave him my necker and he gave me his was something that I think I’ll always remember,” she said. Unfortunately, a combination of a massive heat wave and logistical and sanitation problems led to the UK, U.S. and Singapore Scouting contingents pulling their Scouts from the event after only a few days. U.S. Scouts decamped to Camp Humphreys, a U.S. Army camp about an hour away from Saemangeum on August 5. Then the arrival of Typhoon Khanun led to the evacuation of the remaining tens of thousands of Scouts starting on August 7 to various locations in South Korea. After arriving at Camp Humphreys, the California Scouts persevered in making the most of their experiences. They embarked on trips to local sights, communities, and events, including seeing Photos by Steve Parris, Melissa Schreiner, and Crew 16 Scouts Venturers from Crew 16, including Naomi Treichler (left), explore Gyeongbokgung Palace in Seoul. A few groups of US Scouts were able to tour parts of the Samsung headquarters in Suwon. “I really enjoyed the Samsung employees’ presentations on the technology that they’ve developed there,” said Treichler. articles.text: 1-0 upset victory vs. England a game for the ages How amazing was this year’s Women’s World Cup? In the end, Spain took a 1-0 win over the favorites, England, to capture its first title in the team’s 43-year history. With both England and España fighting as first-timers in the finals, perhaps there is a changing of the guard in the women’s game, which the United States know the field has quickly risen against them. England was bigger, stronger, more experienced, and winner of last year’s Euro Championship. Spain was talented but endured a year of turmoil when more than half of the team chose not to play under coach Jorge Vilda. There were so many illustrious and awe-inspiring moments from this year. Here’s a recap of some of our favorite moments. Spain wins 1-0 over England on Olga Carmona’s goal It’s hard not to view Olga Carmona’s goal in the 29th minute as the pinnacle of the tournament. Spain played fantastically, showing the classic “tiki-taka” style that encapsulates the Spanish-football style. Looking back at Carmona’s game-winner now a few days later, it’s a certain tear-jerker moment. Following the match, she was told by gamily members that her father, Tomas Carmona Mena, had died. When Carmona scored from her left fullback position, the 23-year-old had a separate message, lifting her jersey to reveal “Merchi” written onto her undershirt. She explained it was in honor of a close friend’s mother who had passed away recently. Little to Carmona’s knowledge at the time, her father also had passed. Her shot in the 29th was as perfect as could be to narrowly get past the outstretched arms of England goalkeeper Mary Earps. It was almost as if an angel lent a hand in pushing it into the net. Olga left an emotional message on social media after learning of her father’s passing: “And without knowing it, I had my Star before the game started. I know that you have given me the strength to achieve something unique. I know that you have been watching me tonight and that you are proud of me. articles.text: Richey recounts attaining No. 1 in the U.S. and subsequent work in mental health awareness Originally printed in October 2020. With the French Open now concluded, we take a look back to a former headlining tennis tournament in the Bay Area, the Pacific Coast Championships. in the ‘50s through the early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world played at the Berkeley Tennis Club in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the start of October. The Pacific Coast Championship was held from 1889 to 2013. it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States and is predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of tennis’ Open Era beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championships were in Berkeley from 1968 to 1971. Many influential matches took place for endof-year rankings, given an October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. In 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States. It was a semifinal match at the Pacific Coast Championship that was one of the most breathtaking matches ever played. Their match ran over four hours. and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point the end-all, win-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey, now 73, from his home in San Angelo, Texas. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, which was famously the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix,” Richey said. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals in London. I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my tail was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified in the previous round. “All the players and officials knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an activist for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. In his book, Acing Depression, Richey describes his challenges with the disease in the years following his tennis career. “It’s been a good book from the standpoint of what I wrote it for; if I could help just one person. Clinical depression has 10 or 12 criteria that lasts a various amount of time. It is a bonafide medical illness; it’s like in America we’re allowed to be sick from the Adams Apple down but not the Adams Apple up. It can happen to anybody,” Richey explained. He recounted some of his experiences with depression and what led to him writing the book. “I had episodes throughout my life. In tennis, my last six years of the tour, I had lost my game; I couldn’t get my backhand back,’ he said. “That’s why I got depressed; I had lost what was most valuable to me: my skill… I had a three-year breakdown at my worst,” said Richey, describing some situations from his book. “I’ve spoken at 60 or so events over the last 10 years and hosted some golf events. I wrote the book as a mental health book. The desire was to help others who suffered like I did. It just so happened that my daughter had a year off from being a professor at Texas A&M. She did a wonderful job of Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. putting it together,” he added. Pacific Coast Championship history In 1971, the final year at Berkeley, Australian legends Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall squared off in what became “Rocket” Laver’s sixth singles title of the year. The doubles’ title in ‘71 was another all-Australian exhibit with Laver and Roy Emerson defeating Rosewall and Fred Stolle. It was held in multiple venues starting at the Old Del Monte Lodge in Monterey in 1889, moving to the Hotel Rafael in San Rafael from 1890 to 1899, and then to Berkeley from 1900 to 1930 for its initial stay. From there, the PCC played in Alamo from 1931-1933, returned to Berkeley from 1934-1941, went to San Francisco in ’42-’48, then back to Berkeley from 1949 through 1971. pages.text: Wednesday, August 23, 2023 13 A look back Tennis legend Cliff Richey & the Pacific Coast Championships at the Berkeley Tennis Club Richey recounts attaining No. 1 in the U.S. and subsequent work in mental health awareness By Jonathan Comeaux Originally printed in October 2020. With the French Open now concluded, we take a look back to a former headlining tennis tournament in the Bay Area, the Pacific Coast Championships. in the ‘50s through the early 70s, some of the best tennis players in the world played at the Berkeley Tennis Club in the shadows of the Claremont Hotel at the start of October. The Pacific Coast Championship was held from 1889 to 2013. it was the second oldest ongoing tennis tourney in the United States and is predated only by the U.S. Open. With the start of tennis’ Open Era beginning in 1968, the final three years of the Pacific Coast Championships were in Berkeley from 1968 to 1971. Many influential matches took place for endof-year rankings, given an October championship meant it was among the final tournaments to determine the leaderboard. In 1970, that meant Cliff Richey squaring off with former Wimbledon and US Open champion Stan Smith for the No. 1 ranking in the United States. It was a semifinal match at the Pacific Coast Championship that was one of the most breathtaking matches ever played. Their match ran over four hours. and was perhaps the only time a No. 1 ranking came down to a sudden-death point. The score was 7-6, 6-7, 6-3, 6-4, and 4-4 in the final set with the next point the end-all, win-all. Richey hit a forehand volley for the winner. “Almost any way you cut it, the Pacific Coast Championship in Berkeley was the last event of the year for international players… That year going into the tournament, I knew I was in the running for the No. 1 ranking in the United States,” explained Richey, now 73, from his home in San Angelo, Texas. “That match was such an unusual finish; it went literally down to the last ball. I had a second serve in my hand at four points all, six-all in the fifth set after playing for four hours, it was ridiculous!” added Richey. Richey’s victory over Smith also meant that he was on pace to win tennis’ world point system under the International Tennis Federation’s Grand Prix circuit, which was famously the predecessor of the current ATP Tour. “In addition, that match was also important because that was the first year the International Tennis Federation Grand Prix of tennis, which was a point system and started at the French Open and finished in Europe. I knew at the Berkeley event that I was doing well in the Grand Prix,” Richey said. “I went to Europe after beating Stan and beat Ken Rosewall in the semifinals in London. I knew I had to win two matches in Stockholm the next week. The other player right on my tail was Arthur Ashe, but he had to win Stockholm… So the match against Stan also enabled me to win the Grand Prix,” explained Richey. Richey lost to Hall of Famer Arthur Ashe in the 1970 Pacific Coast Championship finals, but his No. 1 ranking was already solidified in the previous round. “All the players and officials knew that my match with Stan Smith in the semifinals would be for the No. 1 ranking regardless of what happened in the finals,” he said. Following his tennis career, Richey became an activist for mental health awareness after dealing with bouts of clinical depression. In his book, Acing Depression, Richey describes his challenges with the disease in the years following his tennis career. “It’s been a good book from the standpoint of what I wrote it for; if I could help just one person. Clinical depression has 10 or 12 criteria that lasts a various amount of time. It is a bonafide medical illness; it’s like in America we’re allowed to be sick from the Adams Apple down but not the Adams Apple up. It can happen to anybody,” Richey explained. He recounted some of his experiences with depression and what led to him writing the book. “I had episodes throughout my life. In tennis, my last six years of the tour, I had lost my game; I couldn’t get my backhand back,’ he said. “That’s why I got depressed; I had lost what was most valuable to me: my skill… I had a three-year breakdown at my worst,” said Richey, describing some situations from his book. “I’ve spoken at 60 or so events over the last 10 years and hosted some golf events. I wrote the book as a mental health book. The desire was to help others who suffered like I did. It just so happened that my daughter had a year off from being a professor at Texas A&M. She did a wonderful job of Photo courtesy of Cliff Richey A newspaper clipping of Cliff Richey’s sudden-death victory over Stan Smith at the Berkeley Tennis Club’s Pacific Coast Championship in 1970. putting it together,” he added. Pacific Coast Championship history In 1971, the final year at Berkeley, Australian legends Rod Laver and Ken Rosewall squared off in what became “Rocket” Laver’s sixth singles title of the year. The doubles’ title in ‘71 was another all-Australian exhibit with Laver and Roy Emerson defeating Rosewall and Fred Stolle. It was held in multiple venues starting at the Old Del Monte Lodge in Monterey in 1889, moving to the Hotel Rafael in San Rafael from 1890 to 1899, and then to Berkeley from 1900 to 1930 for its initial stay. From there, the PCC played in Alamo from 1931-1933, returned to Berkeley from 1934-1941, went to San Francisco in ’42-’48, then back to Berkeley from 1949 through 1971. The Cow Palace and Bill Graham Civic Auditorium hosted the tournament from 1973 to 1993; then moved to San Jose with the opening of the HP Pavilion. That was its downward phase when it was classified as an ATP 250 series tournament. During its time in San Francisco, John McEnroe dominated the event with 14 combined singles and doubles titles, five in singles. articles.text: Your child’s path in school might take many twists and turns. It’s back to school time! A time when parents are taking a deep breath. While summer can be super fun, it can also be exhausting because there is so much less structure to the schedule. So, back to the day to day it is for kids and their anxious parents. Get up, get ready, shoes on, out the door and into the classroom on time and ready to learn, As school begins, it can become easy to think that the year needs to follow a specific path and have one set outcome for kids. Of course, we all want our kids to do well in school. But, the definition of “do well in school” can be looked at from different perspectives. It could be a prescribed concept that means one specific path, or it could be a developing idea that shifts and changes daily. School is all about learning. And, as a parent, we can get stuck in believing that the learning journey has a set outcome goal– get good grades, do the right activities, and eventually, get into the right college. This is typically how we all think about school. Every day is one more step towards a set outcome. Therefore, if on any given day your child is struggling with an element of the school process, that becomes a problem. The steps are predetermined, so the path is already made and the child must follow that path. Or, we can see the day to day of growing up and developing, and therefore school, as a creative process. The creative path doesn’t know its end point. It’s the process itself that creates and reveals the end point. If there is no already-predetermined outcome goal, the child is creating the path every day. All of a sudden, a struggle is not a moment where we are fearful of a bad grade, but instead becomes a gift because an opportunity for learning has presented itself. A child’s passions can lead the way, and if those passions change, that’s ok too because the passions are also determining the path. as a creative process, it allows the child’s experience to formulate the path one day at a time and it releases the parent from stressing about every setback. It’s the process of attending school that creates the endpoint. As a result, each step the child takes, even if it is a tiny step or a sideways step or, even a step backwards, is creating the path and the outcome. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Speaker, Consultant and Coach. https:// gocreate.zone.

articles.text: I went through Piedmont schools and my emotions about going back to school fluctuated over the years from so excited to see my friends to begging my mom to let me stay home. Does that sound familiar? As summer comes to an end and the hustle and bustle of fall begins, I want to introduce a concept called “negativity bias”. This is the idea that our brains are wired for survival and therefore wired to see the negatives of a situation much more easily than the positives. This was optimal in our primal days where we needed to be aware of danger and threats, but in our current environment it can lead us to unnecessary negativity. Even though there are both negatives and positives about summer ending, it’s so much easier to focus on the negatives. We might think about vacation ending, shorter days, and less free time but forget about the friends we’ll see or the return of the Pumpkin Spice Latte. Understanding that our brains have this bias is the first step to changing it, but simply being aware of it is not enough to become happier. Using Positive Psychology, we can actually rewire our brains to be happier and more productive. Through tools like mindfulness, gratitude, and goal setting, we are able to train our brains to see the positives more often and more easily. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and experience to coach people one-on-one and facilitate workshops on different concepts from Positive Psychology. I found my passion in helping others figure out what they want, who they are, and how to show up more authentically in their lives. Learning these tools from Positive Psychology has completely transformed my life, and I feel so lucky to be able to help other people find that joy. If you have been waiting for a sign to do something different this year, this might be it. Positive Psychology is not the idea that we need to be happy all the time but instead the concept that we are happy a lot of the time and just need a little help noticing it. articles.text: The story of a pair of sturdy stilettos Berkeley Playhouse opens its 2023-24 season with the Tonyaward winning musical Kinky Boots opening on September 8. Kinky Boots protagonist Charlie Price inherits his father’s beleaguered and nearly bankrupt shoe factory. He finds inspiration in customer Lola, a provocative entertainer, who wants to purchase a pair of sturdy stilettos. An unlikely pair, Charlie and Lola find they have more in common than they initially thought. The uplifting play features music and lyrics by Cyndi Lauper and is based on the 2005 British film of the same name, written by Geoff Deane and Tim Firth and mostly inspired by true events. “It’s just a heartfelt, heartwarming show about community and that’s exactly what Berkeley Playhouse is about. It’s perfect,” Director William Thomas Hodgson said. “The vision is a celebration of queerness, a community in queerness. Tshow has been on Broadway, on the West End, and around the world, I feel like we have our own special sauce in Berkeley.” The cast includes B Noel Thomas playing both Lola and Simon, Seth Hanson as Charlie Price, Grace Margaret Craig as Nicola, No’Eau Kahalekulu as Lauren, Danny Cozart as Don and Maia Campbell as Pat. The musical will be performed through October 15. Performances run Friday through Sunday, and select weekday evenings, beginning September 8. articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum is now exhibiting Hell: Arts of Asian Underworlds through September 18. The new exhibition displays how different Asian cultures view the afterlife of the condemned over time. Hell exhibits over 40 paintings, sculptures, maps, puppets, and religious objects from India, Tibet, China, Korea, Japan, Indonesia, Thailand, Myanmar, and the Philippines. “There is a presumption that all representations of Hell across Asian cultures are the same or continuous,” said Jeff Durham, Curator of Himalayan Art at the Asian Art Museum. “But in fact, whether they appear in ancient traditions or the work of contemporary artists, depictions of Hell have been extraordinarily diverse: some are terrifying and gruesome, but many are humorous and playful.” The majority of artworks on view are on loan from other institutions and collections. Pieces owned by the museum are newly acquired and are being shown for the first time. “This exhibition is like a rollercoaster taking the visitor from excitement to relief; in the end, it shows that Hell is only as bad as we imagine it to be,” Durham said. Visit https://exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/hell-arts-ofasian-underworlds/ to learn more and purchase museum passes. The museum is located at 200 Larkin Street, a block from City Hall. These vary in size from immense paved open spaces to planted park-like piazzas. At the scale of the biggest, the spaces are mostly suited for ceremonial or ritual activities involving large numbers of people, and are surrounded by mostly civic buildings. The smallest scale found in most intimate town or village plazas typically contains more interactive civic spaces surrounded by restaurants, shopping and some smaller government functions. There exist important and even critical requirements for all these different essential places to be successful: these are essential design concepts that must be adopted to the specific layout, use, orientation, geography, size and culture of a place. There are no pat examples that can be copied indiscriminately. The concept of “enclosure” (forming “outdoor rooms”) that we have discussed before applies at all scales. Without surrounding buildings, or trees, or geographical features that define the limits or edges of these outdoor plaza spaces it is difficult to really mark them as the heart of the municipality. There also seems to exist a sense of order and even comfort to the spaces that are clearly bounded. Attractions and destinations Now a museum and tourist attraction, the Forbidden City in the heart of Beijing was the ceremonial and political center of the Chinese government. The preserved wood buildings are marvelous in stature and detail; they were and do inspire awe. But to my mind the place is compromised by the excessive undefined open space around them – a lack of urban design.

articles.text: It’s still summer, so enjoy the freshness of tomatoes Photos by Deborah Quok Pan con tomate is an ideal summer snack for any time of the day. Throughout Spain is eaten throughout the day – breakfast through tapas time. The dish is simply plated – fresh tomato on toasted bread; with a rub of fresh garlic, a splash of extra-virgin olive oil, and a sprinkle of salt for additional flavor. Regular readers have likely noticed what a fan I am of Spanish cuisine. I’ve had the good fortune to visit the diverse country many times, starting back in the late ‘90s. I’ve experienced pan con tomate set-ups at breakfast buffets, on lunch, tapas and dinner menus, and my personal favorite, at the beachside restaurants in Menorca. This dish makes an appearance from humble to haute settings. For such a simple recipe, I have had the misfortune of subpar offerings. Here’s my technique that ensures crusty bread and supreme tomatoey-ness with unctuous textures and popping flavor. Since there are so few ingredients, quality is key: select the tastiest bread and tomatoes you can find; and the best extra-virgin olive oil whose flavor will enhance the tomatoes. The Bay Area and Central Spain share a similar latitude, so farming crops are similar. Think citrus, olives, nut trees, grapes, and the star of this dish – tomatoes. It’s peak tomato season now and since my paltry container tomato crop doesn’t fill our needs, I’m taking full advantage of what our farmers’ markets have to offer. Advance note: The resulting recipe quantity will vary depending on the size of your tomatoes, their juiciness and the size of the bread used. Scale the ingredients to suit your situation. Pan con Tomate – Spanish Style Bread with Tomatoes Makes about 1/2 cup of tomato topping, good for about 8 pieces INGREDIENTS • 2 medium-large tomatoes, select firm-ripe ones at peak flavor • 1 large clove garlic • 2 - 4 tablespoons extra-virgin olive oil • 1 teaspoon sea salt • 1 loaf baguette, or other firm, crusty bread INSTRUCTIONS Cut the tomatoes in half crosswise. Using the large holes of a box grater, carefully grate the fleshy side into a bowl. You should only have the thin skin remaining. This will yield about one cup of grated tomato. Pour the grated tomato through a fine mesh strainer into another bowl, reserving the juice to add back as needed to create a tomato spread with the viscosity of a jam or jelly. Cut the baguette into 3-inch lengths, then slice each piece in half crosswise. Place the sliced pieces cut side up and broil until lightly toasted, about 4 minutes. (A toaster oven is ideal here.) Rub the clove of garlic across the toasted bread. Start on the crispier edges to break through the garlic. Go lightly as this method imparts a lot of garlickiness, and you want to have the tomatoes shine here. Spread the jammy, fresh tomato onto each piece. Drizzle each piece with extra-virgin olive oil and sprinkle with sea salt. Serve immediately. Some absorption of the tomatoes into the bread is desired, but you want to avoid soggy bread.
articles.title: Pan con Tomate – Bread with Tomato

articles.text: A Walking on Wednesdays group 30 walkers and one k-9 best friend headed out on another uphill trek, this time to see the EBMUD’s Piedmont “Reservoir Number 2” at the top of Dudley and Blair Avenues. There was some elevation going up Dudley, but it is a long, slow climb. The group started out taking shortcut path from Piedmont Court to Mountain Avenue. They passed a front yard with a life-size sculpture of a distinguished looking gentleman in a leaf-like coat, something like the Stanford Tree. The walkers continued on, and turned up the long, steep Dudley Avenue. They took a side trip onto the Dudley Court cul-de-sac to catch their breaths, and arrived at the reservoir one block away. It is far above Blair Park and occupies more than nine acres straddling the Oakland-Piedmont border with 8.3 acres of in Piedmont. A 22.8 million gallon water storage tank provided water for Piedmont from 1905 to 2003. The facility was decommissioned and drained in 2003 as part of EBMUD’s facility modernization program. Piedmont’s water now comes from other large tanks in the Oakland Hills. Jim Kellogg told the group that the land was once considered for residential development, but with parts of it in Piedmont and Oakland, the approval process was too complicated. A shelter and bench provided a respite from the rising temperature, and the backdrop for a group photo. There were more streets nearby that could have been explored, but the group chose to save those for a future day. They descended to the middle of town on Mountain and Hager, with spectacular views of the Bay. A breeze was welcomed too. It was about a two mile walk over about one hour and offered some good exercise. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Don Parachini, a longtime Piedmont resident passed away on July 1, 2023. Born Donald Gene Parachini, he was the son of Victor and Elma Parachini of Antioch, CA. He attended school in Antioch and was on the high school football, track, and wrestling teams. While growing up he developed a great love of the outdoors, especially hunting ducks and pheasants and fishing in the Delta. His interest in the outdoors led him to enroll at Washington State University in Pullman as a forestry major, eventually changing to a major in business and economics. He continued to wrestle and was co-captain of the team his senior year. Don had a lifelong love of learning on wide-ranging topics and was an avid reader. He maintained his college friendships and later served as a member of the Board of Governors and Gift Acceptance and Management committee of the WSU Foundation. Following graduation from college, Don and his father took a lengthy tour through Europe. While there, they made contact with cousins for the first time since WWI. This experience heightened his interest in his Italian heritage and a desire to further expand his Italian language skills. He read many of the Italian classics and the local San Francisco Italian newspaper. He cultivated friends often over a long meal or a glass of wine in North Beach. Upon returning from his trip to Europe Don received an invitation from the Army to report for duty at Fort Ord. Don entered as a private but liked the military life and enrolled in the Officer Candidate School in Fort Sill, Oklahoma. As a freshly minted lieutenant in the artillery, he was sent back to Fort Ord where he spent much of his time at Hunter Ligget. It’s really difficult for them to return to the wild by themselves. They have a really big brain, so when they are used to being fed by people, it’s hard for them to find their own food because they know humans will feed them,” explained Mike, a guide at Into The Wild. After feeding the elephants, visitors were offered a brief hike through the jungle alongside the elephants, observing how they naturally live in the wild—finding dirt pits to throw on themselves and trees to topple as they scratch their backsides. Guides also pointed out edible foliage for foraging and how local tribes have used different species of plants for uses as medicine, insect repellent, and cuisine. This hike put us in close quarters with the Thailand wilderness. Getting back to Into The Wild’s camp, a typical July-monsoon swept over the area. It was breathtaking to watch and listen to the downpour of rain slam on the metal roof of out platform. When the rain passed, our group made medicine balls to help the elephants’ digestive systems using the camp’s mortar and pestle system before jumping into the Mae Tian River to coat the elephants with mud. After a brief swim in the river without the elephants, it was time to call it a day and make the trek back to Chiang Mai.

Gran Moraine Taking its name from the glacier movements in the last Ice Age, the Missoula Floods deposited glacial sediment (moraines) in the northern Willamette Valley. Located in the heart of the Yamhill-Carlton AVA in the Willamette Valley, Gran Moraine produces Chardonnay and Pinot Noir from a 190-acre estate vineyard. The winery which is part of the Jackson Family of wineries purchased the Zena Crown vineyard in the Eola-Amty Hills AVA in 2013. We met winemaker Shane Moore there one bright, sunny morning for a tour of this exquisite property. The perfectly manicured hills of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir are cooled by Pacific Ocean air that comes through the Van Duzer Corridor, a gap in the coastal mountain range. Back at the Gran Moraine main tasting room we worked our way through three sparkling wines, concluding with the 2015 Gran Moraine Blanc de Blanc, a magnificent sparkler with great beauty and depth. It was the best sparkling wine of the trip. They also poured a now seriously trendy “orange wine” – the 2021 Flavorscape Pinot Blanc. Orange wines are white wines made in the style of red wines with extended skin contact during the fermentation. The wine was perky and fresh with intriguing earthy flavors. We had three of the Zena Crown Pinot Noirs – all were big, intense wines with a Burgundian complexity to the nose and the capacity to age for decades. Gran Moraine also produces a lovely Chardonnay, the 2019 Yamhill/ Carlton Chardonnay, which had the perfect touch of sweet vanilla oak on the nose and a long savory finish. The entire experience at Gran Moraine from the wonderful tour of Zena Crown that Shane Moore gave us to the charming friendly hospitality of the tasting room staff made our visit a truly pleasant one. FAVORITE WINE 2019 Gran Moraine Dropstone Pinot Noir The wine offers layered scents of cherries, cranberries, licorice and underbrush. Medium bodied, its concentrated berry fruit boasts layer after layer of spicy, earthy accents with a seamless frame and impressive length. something that would not only serve consumers, but also the longevity of the state he calls home. Utilizing organic farming methods and gravity flow production, Lemelson crafts estate grown Pinot Noir, Pinot Gris, Chardonnay and Riesling. Lemelson owns and manages multiple sites in the Northern Willamette Valley, with vineyards that span three AVAs with numerous soil types, exposures, and elevations. The Lemelson tasting room is comfy and cozy with tastings also offered outdoors. We were hosted by Sales and Operations manager Devon Elstun who was extremely knowledgeable about the winery history and current practices in addition to the wines. After a week of drinking almost exclusively Pinot Noir and Chardonnay it was refreshing to get to try the Lemelson 2022 Riesling, a dry wine from the Dundee Hills. The nose was all grapefruit and pineapple with medium body and good fruit. It could use a touch more acid. I also enjoyed their 2022 Chestnut Hill Pinot Gris which was floral, soft and round with apricot and peach flavors. The 2021 Lemelson Chardonnay had some vanilla oak in the nose alongside apple and pear flavors with great balance and structure. The tasting experience at Lemelson is very laid back with warm hospitality from the entire staff. Highly recommended. It has layered aromas; cranberries, blueberries and earth are complemented by shifting tones of sage, lilac and black pepper. The medium-bodied palate is just as alluring, with powerful layers of spicy fruit. It has great structure and a long finish. articles.text: Seriously? We Just Got Cancelled!? Last month, like a number of our neighbors and clients, my husband and I found a cancellation notice in the mail from our home insurance provider. In our case, the reason for the cancellation was not clear. Is it the type of roof on our home? Is it the size of our home? Are there too many trees on our parcel? Prompted by this notice, I reached out to a seasoned insurance broker, Steven Klein of Greystone Insurance, seeking more information on the primary reasons for cancellations in the marketplace. Steven’s insight can be found in the side bar. What should you do if you received a notice of cancellation? First, contact the company or Broker that you worked with on the policy and see if they can assist in preventing the cancellation. Keeping your current insurance may be the best path forward because if you go to a different company, they may require an inspection of your home and decide not to offer a policy because of the four items listed. Nonrenewal rate of all homeowner policies Old Home Systems or Systems in Disrepair Condition is important. Having the major systems in your home relatively updated can be critical. Some insurance companies are using artificial intelligence (AI) and drawing from public records to determine the age of, say, a roof. If they see that the last permit for a roof replacement was 40 years ago, they may ask for proof that the roof has been replaced recently or cancel the policy if the roof is not replaced. Neighborhood Risk Designations Changing Insurance companies are changing their mapping for risks like fire. Steven has a client in the Berkeley Hills whose home was not originally considered high-fire risk, now it is. Some insurance companies are working to move out of areas considered higher risk and may either raise the cost of policies annually or cancel them altogether. Defensible Space and Brush Clearance For policy renewal, some companies are requiring that brush and trees around the subject property be cleared. Of course, in several of our local cities certain types of trees are protected, like oak trees in Berkeley, which creates a challenge for the homeowner if the insurance company requires the tree to be cut down but the local city will not permit its removal. Submitting a Claim Exercise caution when making a claim on your home insurance. Companies can increase your rates or drop you for making even one claim. Consider whether the consequences of making the claim merit the financial burden of the item for which the claim is being made. This includes nonrenewals and cancellations initiated by the consumer or the insurer. Chart: Sriharsha Devulapalli/The Chronicle. Source: CA Dept of Insurance. Second, if you worked directly with a company like State Farm or Allstate and they are going to cancel your policy, try reaching out to an insurance broker. Insurance brokers are different in that they often sell policies for 10-20 different companies and can look for one who insures homes in your neighborhood and will do so at the lowest cost. In the end, our insurance broker worked with the company to maintain the policy on our home. The rate increased by nearly 25%, however, in this insurance environment, keeping the policy we have on the home seems like the prudent choice. Thank you to Steven for taking the time to share his knowledge and insights about insurance with us. can be found at https://www.greystoneinsured.com. He Some homeowners and homebuyers have resorted to the California Fair Plan, which is generally more costly, but unless the state’s insurance commissioner can get more private insurers to write policies in high risk areas, it may end up being the only property insurance available.
